bai.moTa: Space stretches, with no center; the Friedmann equation; accelerating expansion
bai.yChinh: Apply Einstein’s equation to the whole universe and you get a shocking result: the universe cannot stand still; it must expand or contract. Every large distance is proportional to a single factor $a(t)$, and galaxies recede from one another at speeds proportional to their distance. Space has been stretching like this for **13.8 billion years**, and for the last 6 billion years or so it has been stretching **faster and faster**.
bai.giaiThich:
Galaxies recede with $v = H_0 d$, where $H_0 \approx 67{,}4$ km/s per megaparsec. They are not flying through space: **space itself is stretching**, and every large distance is multiplied by the same factor $a(t)$. Observers in any galaxy see the same thing, so there is no center.

Light traveling through expanding space is stretched: $1 + z = 1/a$. The Friedmann equation $H^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - kc^2/a^2$ links the expansion rate to the density; the critical density $3H_0^2/(8\pi G) \approx 8{,}5 \times 10^{-27}$ kg/m³ is about 5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter.

Radiation thins out as $a^{-4}$, matter as $a^{-3}$, and dark energy not at all. The acceleration equation $\ddot a/a = -\tfrac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3P/c^2)$ shows that dark energy (negative pressure) makes the expansion accelerate, starting when $a = (\Omega_m/2\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3} \approx 0{,}61$, about 6.1 billion years ago. Integrating gives the age of the universe: 13.8 billion years.
bai.conSo.1: **67.4 km/s per megaparsec**: the Hubble constant from Planck; distance-ladder measurements give about 73 (the “Hubble tension”).
bai.conSo.2: **13.8 billion years**: the age of the universe in ΛCDM (Planck 2018: 13.79). By comparison, $1/H_0 = 14{,}5$ billion years.
bai.conSo.3: **8.5 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³**: the critical density, about 5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter.
bai.conSo.4: **5% – 27% – 68%**: ordinary matter, dark matter and dark energy in today’s universe.
bai.conSo.5: **6.1 billion years ago** ($z \approx 0{,}63$): the expansion switched from decelerating to accelerating.
bai.conSo.6: **2.725 K**: the temperature of the background radiation today; it was emitted at $z \approx 1\,090$, when the universe was about 380,000 years old.
bai.hieuDung: **Galaxies are not “flying” through space; space itself is stretching.** That is why very distant galaxies can recede faster than light without breaking relativity. The Big Bang did not happen at one point but everywhere. Tightly bound things such as atoms, Earth, the Solar System and even whole galaxies do **not** expand; that is why the galaxies in the model keep their size.
bai.nguon: Cosmological parameters: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6 (H0 = 67.4 ± 0.5; Ωm = 0.315; Ωb·h² = 0.0224; age 13.79 billion years; z = 1,090). H0 of about 73 from the distance ladder: the SH0ES team (Riess et al. 2022); about 70 with the James Webb Space Telescope: Freedman et al. 2025. Hints of evolving dark energy: DESI 2025 (DR2). Accelerating expansion: Riess et al. 1998, Perlmutter et al. 1999. Lemaître 1927, Hubble 1929. Derivations follow Ryden (2016), Hartle (2003) ch. 17–18, Baez and Bunn 2005, Davis and Lineweaver 2004. The numbers are recomputed in kiem-tra/kiem-song-va-gian-no.mjs.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.1: State and use the Hubble–Lemaître law $v = H_0 d$, including converting the unit km/s per megaparsec.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.2: Explain why the expansion has no center, and clear up three misconceptions: the Big Bang happened at a point, receding faster than light is impossible, and everything expands.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.3: Use the scale factor $a(t)$ to compute redshift: $1 + z = 1/a$.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.4: Derive a Newtonian version of the Friedmann equation, compute the critical density, and connect the acceleration equation to the $\rho + 3P/c^2$ statement of Lesson 12.
bai.baiGiang.mucTieu.5: Say why the data favor the ΛCDM model, when the universe began to accelerate, and what the “Hubble tension” is.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.noiDung:
Each galaxy drawn here stands for a cluster of galaxies. The galaxy inside the gold ring in the middle is your **home galaxy**. The blue arrows show how fast the clusters around it are receding: a cluster twice as far away has an arrow twice as long. The graph below the control panel plots velocity against distance: a straight line.

That is the {{định luật Hubble–Lemaître|Hubble–Lemaître law}}:

$$ v = H_0\, d . $$

$d$ is the distance, $v$ the recession velocity, and $H_0$ today’s {{hằng số Hubble|Hubble constant}}. The Planck satellite gives $H_0 \approx 67{,}4$ km/s per megaparsec (1 Mpc = 3.26 million light-years).

> [Ví dụ] A galaxy 100 Mpc away recedes at $67{,}4 \times 100 = 6\,740$ km/s. Its light is stretched by about 2.2% (redshift $z \approx v/c \approx 0{,}022$).

The gold line joins home to a **sample galaxy**: its label gives that galaxy’s distance and velocity, in exact proportion $H_0$.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the gold dot on the **sample galaxy** farther away or closer: twice as far means twice the recession speed. Hover over any galaxy to read its distance and velocity. With sound on you hear two notes: the reference note played at home, then the note received from the sample galaxy, lower because of the redshift (step 3).
> [[Velocity–distance graph|hubble]] [[Close-up view|gan]] [[Wide view|tong]]

> [Lưu ý] The galaxies are drawn hundreds of times larger than they really are so you can see them; their spiral or elliptical shapes are illustrations. Their sizes do not grow with the universe (step 8 explains why).

> [Lịch sử] In 1927 Georges Lemaître derived from Einstein’s equation that the universe is expanding and that recession velocity must be proportional to distance. In 1929 Edwin Hubble published measurements of galaxy distances showing exactly that. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended the name Hubble–Lemaître law.

+++ Go deeper: $1/H_0$ is a time scale
$H_0$ has units of (km/s)/Mpc, that is, “per second.” Using 1 Mpc $= 3{,}086 \times 10^{19}$ km:

$$ \frac{1}{H_0} = \frac{3{,}086 \times 10^{19}\ \text{km}}{67{,}4\ \text{km/s}} \approx 4{,}6 \times 10^{17}\ \text{s} \approx 14{,}5\ \text{billion yr}. $$

If every galaxy had always kept its present velocity, $d/v = 1/H_0$ would be the time since they were all together: 14.5 billion years. The true age computed carefully (step 7) is 13.8 billion years; the closeness of the two numbers is largely a coincidence, because the expansion first slowed down and then sped up. Likewise $c/H_0 \approx 4\,450$ Mpc, about 14.5 billion light-years, is called the Hubble distance.

The model ignores each galaxy’s own peculiar motion (a few hundred km/s), so the points on the graph lie exactly on a straight line; real data scatter around that line, especially nearby.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.de: Drag the sample galaxy to where it **today** recedes at exactly **half the speed of light** (to within 0.03 c).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.1.thuThach.goiY: $v = H_0 d$, so you need $d = 0{,}5\, c/H_0 \approx 7{,}3$ billion light-years (about 2,220 Mpc). The sample galaxy’s label updates as you drag.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.ten: Space stretches: no center, no edge
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.noiDung:
Look at the glowing grid: it stretches along with the galaxies. Galaxy clusters **are not flying through space**; each stays almost at rest in its own place, while the distance between every pair is multiplied by the same factor. It is like a loaf of raisin bread rising: every raisin sees all the others moving away, and the farther a raisin is, the faster it recedes.

So there is **no center**. Click any galaxy in the scene (or the button below) to “move house” there: from your new home you see exactly the same picture, with everything receding from you according to $v = H_0 d$.

> [Thử ngay] [[Move to another galaxy|chuyen]] [[Back to the original home|ve]] [[Play from the Big Bang|chieu]]

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “The Big Bang was an explosion at a point, and galaxies are the debris flying outward.” Not so. There was no point of explosion and no “outside” to fly into. Every place in space was once equally dense and hot, and every place expanded. The Big Bang happened **everywhere at once**.

> [Lưu ý] The model is a repeating box: leave through one side and you come back through the opposite side, so there is no edge and every galaxy sees the same view. The real universe may be finite without an edge, or infinite; current data cannot tell which.

+++ Go deeper: why only $v \propto d$ has no center
Let $D$ be the {{khoảng cách đồng chuyển|comoving distance}} (the distance measured today, constant in time) and $a(t)$ the common factor. The proper distance at time $t$ is $d = a(t)\,D$. Taking the time derivative:

$$ v = \dot a\, D = \frac{\dot a}{a}\, d = H\, d, \qquad H = \frac{\dot a}{a}. $$

Stand at galaxy B instead of A: the velocity of C relative to B is $v_C - v_B = H(d_C - d_B)$, still the Hubble law, now centered on B. If velocity were proportional to $d^2$, say, the subtraction would no longer keep that form: observers in each galaxy would see a different picture, and there would be a special “center.” A homogeneous universe (the same everywhere) and isotropic universe (the same in every direction) forces the expansion to take the form $v = Hd$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.de: Click directly on **two different galaxies** in the scene to move house twice. After each move, look at the arrows: every galaxy still recedes from your new home.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.2.thuThach.goiY: Hover over a galaxy: the tooltip says “Click to move house here.” The “Move” button in the lesson does not count.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.noiDung:
The model is now at the moment when the universe was 5.8 billion years old and every large distance was only **half** of today’s: {{hệ số tỉ lệ|scale factor}} $a = 0{,}5$. By convention $a = 1$ today. Every distance between galaxy clusters is $d = a(t)\,D$, with $D$ fixed.

Light traveling through expanding space is stretched along with it: wavelength is proportional to $a$. Light emitted when the scale factor was $a$ reaches us today with a wavelength $1/a$ times longer. That is the {{dịch chuyển đỏ vũ trụ học|cosmological redshift}}:

$$ 1 + z = \frac{\lambda_\text{obs}}{\lambda_\text{em}} = \frac{1}{a_\text{em}} . $$

> [Ví dụ] Light emitted at $a = 0{,}5$ has $z = 1$: the red line of hydrogen (656 nm) reaches us at 1,312 nm, in the infrared. At $a = 0{,}25$ (when the universe was 2.1 billion years old), $z = 3$.

Turn on **redshift coloring**: each galaxy is tinted by the redshift of the light from it reaching home at this moment. The farther away, the longer the light has traveled and the more it has been stretched.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the blue dot on the **cosmic clock** (the vertical column at the home galaxy) to change the time: the grid, the galaxies and the coloring change with it. Turn on sound to hear the sample galaxy’s beep drop in pitch.
> [[At a = 0.5|a05]] [[At a = 0.25|a025]] [[Back to today|nay]] [[Toggle redshift coloring|do]]

> [Lưu ý] The tint is a conventional color scale for $z$ (white, orange, deep red), not what the eye would see: at $z$ around 1, visible light has already become infrared. The beep is likewise translated so the ear can hear it: the hydrogen red line ($4{,}57 \times 10^{14}$ Hz) is mapped to an 880 Hz note played at home; the note received from the sample galaxy has frequency $880/(1 + z)$ Hz and its beats are spaced $1 + z$ times farther apart, just as the light wave is stretched.

> [Con số] The {{bức xạ nền vi sóng vũ trụ|background radiation}} was emitted at $z \approx 1\,090$, when the universe was about 380,000 years old and at about 3,000 K. Its wavelength has been stretched 1,091 times, and its temperature has dropped by the same factor, to 2.725 K today.

+++ Go deeper: why wavelength is proportional to $a$
Two successive wave crests leave the source a very short time $\Delta t_\text{em}$ apart. In a time $\dd t$ light covers a comoving distance $\dd D = c\,\dd t / a(t)$. Both crests travel the same comoving distance, so

$$ \frac{c\,\Delta t_\text{em}}{a_\text{em}} = \frac{c\,\Delta t_\text{obs}}{a_\text{obs}} \ \Rightarrow\ \frac{\lambda_\text{obs}}{\lambda_\text{em}} = \frac{a_\text{obs}}{a_\text{em}} . $$

No velocity appears in this formula. So $z$ should not be thought of as the Doppler effect of some velocity at emission; for large $z$, both $v = cz$ and the special-relativistic Doppler formula give wrong results (see Davis and Lineweaver 2004). Only for small $z$ is $z \approx v/c$, as in step 1.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.de: Drag the cosmic clock to the moment when light emitted then reaches us today with redshift $z = 2$ (to within 0.15).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.3.thuThach.goiY: $1 + z = 1/a$, so you need $a = 1/3$: every distance one third of today’s, when the universe was about 3.3 billion years old. The readout shows $z$ directly.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.noiDung:
Where does the expansion rate come from? Applying Einstein’s equation (Lesson 12) to a homogeneous, isotropic universe, Alexander Friedmann (1922) obtained

$$ H^2 = \left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\,\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} . $$

$\rho$ is the density of everything (matter, radiation, dark energy; energy divided by $c^2$), and $k$ describes the curvature of space. This is the {{phương trình Friedmann|Friedmann equation}}. It looks exactly like energy conservation for a stone thrown upward: kinetic energy (left side) balances gravitational potential energy (the $\rho$ term) and the “total energy” (the $k$ term).

Space is flat ($k = 0$) when $\rho$ equals the {{mật độ tới hạn|critical density}}

$$ \rho_c = \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G} \approx 8{,}5 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg/m}^3 , $$

about **5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter**. Densities are expressed with the {{tham số mật độ|density parameter}} $\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$. Planck finds a total $\Omega$ equal to 1 within a few thousandths: the universe is very nearly flat.

> [Thử ngay] The graph below the panel is $a(t)$ solved from this equation. Compare the real universe with an overdense one that recollapses: choose “Too much matter,” then drag the cosmic clock upward; the grid’s expansion slows, stops, then reverses.
> [[Real universe|thuc]] [[Too much matter|dong]] [[Matter only|vc]]

+++ Go deeper: a Newtonian derivation from a ball of dust
Take an imaginary sphere of radius $R(t) = a(t)\,r$ in a universe filled with uniform dust of density $\rho$. The mass inside, $M = \tfrac43 \pi R^3 \rho$, stays constant as the sphere expands. By the shell theorem, matter outside exerts no net pull on a galaxy sitting on the surface. That galaxy’s energy (per unit mass) is conserved:

$$ \tfrac12 \dot R^2 - \frac{GM}{R} = E . $$

Substitute $M$ and divide by $\tfrac12 R^2 = \tfrac12 a^2 r^2$:

$$ \left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho + \frac{2E}{r^2 a^2} . $$

Setting $2E/r^2 = -kc^2$ gives the Friedmann equation. $E \lt 0$ ($k > 0$): it expands to a maximum and then recollapses, like a stone not thrown hard enough. $E > 0$: it expands forever. $E = 0$ is exactly the case $\rho = \rho_c$.

Plugging in $H_0 = 67{,}4$ km/s/Mpc $= 2{,}18 \times 10^{-18}$ s⁻¹: $\rho_c = 3 \times (2{,}18 \times 10^{-18})^2 / (8\pi \times 6{,}67 \times 10^{-11}) \approx 8{,}5 \times 10^{-27}$ kg/m³. Dividing by the mass of a hydrogen atom, $1{,}67 \times 10^{-27}$ kg, gives about 5.1.

General relativity gives exactly this equation, with two things Newton lacked: $k$ is the real curvature of space, and $\rho$ includes the energy of radiation and dark energy.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.de: With “Too much matter,” drag the cosmic clock to the moment the universe **stops expanding**, just before it starts to contract ($|H| \lt 3$ km/s per megaparsec).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.4.thuThach.goiY: Click “Too much matter,” then drag the blue dot upward. This universe is largest, 1.67 times today’s size, when it is about 31 billion years old; at that moment the “Expansion rate” readout is close to 0.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.ten: Three components, three ways of thinning out
bai.baiGiang.buoc.5.noiDung:
The graph now shows the density of the three components against the scale factor (both axes in powers of 10):

- **Matter** (5% ordinary matter, 27% {{vật chất tối|dark matter}}): the number of particles is fixed and the volume grows as $a^3$, so $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$.
- **Radiation**: the number of photons also thins out as $a^{-3}$, and in addition each photon’s wavelength is stretched so it loses energy as $1/a$: $\rho_r \propto a^{-4}$.
- **Dark energy** in the form of a {{hằng số vũ trụ|cosmological constant}}: its density **stays the same** no matter how much space expands.

Today $\Omega_r \approx 9 \times 10^{-5}$, $\Omega_m = 0{,}315$, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0{,}685$. Going back in time, radiation grows fastest, so the universe has passed through three eras:

| Era | Lasted until | Approximate $a(t)$ |
|---|---|---|
| radiation-dominated | $z \approx 3\,400$, age about 50,000 years | $\propto t^{1/2}$ |
| matter-dominated | $z \approx 0{,}3$, about 3.5 billion years ago | $\propto t^{2/3}$ |
| dark-energy-dominated | ongoing | grows exponentially |

> [Thử ngay] [[When matter equals dark energy|bang]] [[Play from the Big Bang|chieu]] [[Back to today|nay]]

+++ Go deeper: how each component thins out, from energy conservation
A comoving volume $V \propto a^3$ expands like a piston in a cylinder, with no heat flowing in: $\dd(\rho c^2 V) = -P\,\dd V$. For a substance with $P = w\rho c^2$ (constant $w$), the solution is

$$ \rho \propto a^{-3(1+w)} . $$

- Dust, cold matter: $P \approx 0$, $w = 0$, $\rho \propto a^{-3}$.
- Radiation: $P = \rho c^2/3$, $w = 1/3$, $\rho \propto a^{-4}$.
- Cosmological constant: $P = -\rho c^2$, $w = -1$, $\rho$ constant. Negative pressure means that as the volume grows, the work $-P\,\dd V$ is positive: just enough to “fill” the new volume at the same density.

The two milestones in the table: radiation equals matter when $\Omega_r a^{-4} = \Omega_m a^{-3}$, that is $a = \Omega_r/\Omega_m \approx 2{,}9 \times 10^{-4}$; matter equals dark energy when $a = (\Omega_m/\Omega_\Lambda)^{1/3} \approx 0{,}77$.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.6.noiDung:
The curve $a(t)$ on the graph first bends downward (decelerating expansion), then curls upward (accelerating expansion). The white dot sits exactly at the inflection: the universe is **7.7 billion years old**, about **6.1 billion years ago**, $z \approx 0{,}63$.

The reason lies in the statement from Lesson 12: a freely falling ball of particles shrinks according to $\rho + 3P/c^2$, not just $\rho$. For the whole universe this becomes the {{phương trình gia tốc|acceleration equation}}:

$$ \frac{\ddot a}{a} = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho + \frac{3P}{c^2}\right). $$

For matter, $P \approx 0$: the right side is negative and the expansion is braked. For dark energy, $P = -\rho_\Lambda c^2$, so $\rho + 3P/c^2 = -2\rho_\Lambda \lt 0$: it **pushes**. Matter thins out while dark energy does not, so eventually the push wins:

$$ \rho_m = 2\rho_\Lambda \ \Rightarrow\ a = \left(\frac{\Omega_m}{2\Omega_\Lambda}\right)^{1/3} \approx 0{,}613 . $$

> [Thử ngay] Watch the readout change from “decelerating” to “accelerating.” Drag the cosmic clock back and forth around 7.7 billion years to see the switch.
> [[At 4 billion years|truoc]] [[Right at the switch|dung]] [[At 11 billion years|sau]]

> [Lịch sử] In 1998 two teams (Riess et al.; Perlmutter et al.) measured distant {{siêu tân tinh loại Ia|type Ia supernovae}}. These explosions have nearly the same true brightness, so their faintness tells their distance. They were fainter than expected in a decelerating universe: the expansion is **accelerating**. Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.

+++ Go deeper: deriving the acceleration equation
Write the Friedmann equation as $\dot a^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho a^2 - kc^2$ and differentiate with respect to time:

$$ 2\dot a \ddot a = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\left(\dot\rho a^2 + 2\rho a \dot a\right). $$

Energy conservation from step 5, $\dd(\rho c^2 a^3) = -P\,\dd(a^3)$, can be rewritten as $\dot\rho = -3\dfrac{\dot a}{a}\left(\rho + \dfrac{P}{c^2}\right)$. Substitute and divide by $2a\dot a$:

$$ \frac{\ddot a}{a} = \frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(-3\rho - \frac{3P}{c^2} + 2\rho\right) = -\frac{4\pi G}{3}\left(\rho + \frac{3P}{c^2}\right). $$

This is exactly the result Baez and Bunn (2005) use to explain Einstein’s equation: the volume of a ball of test particles shrinks with an acceleration proportional to $\rho + 3P/c^2$. In ΛCDM, with $\rho_m \propto a^{-3}$ and $\rho_\Lambda$ constant, $\ddot a = 0$ when $\Omega_m a^{-3} = 2\Omega_\Lambda$. With $\Omega_m = 0{,}315$, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0{,}685$: $a = 0{,}613$, $z = 1/a - 1 \approx 0{,}63$; integrating $a(t)$ puts that moment 7.7 billion years after the Big Bang.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.7.noiDung:
Once you know $H(a)$ you can compute the age of the universe: add up the time it takes $a$ to grow from 0 to 1,

$$ t_0 = \int_0^1 \frac{\dd a}{a\,H(a)}, $$

$$ H(a) = H_0\sqrt{\Omega_r a^{-4} + \Omega_m a^{-3} + \Omega_k a^{-2} + \Omega_\Lambda} , $$

with $\Omega_k = 1 - \Omega_r - \Omega_m - \Omega_\Lambda$. With the same $H_0 = 67{,}4$, each kind of universe has a different age:

| Kind of universe | Age today | Future |
|---|---|---|
| Real universe (ΛCDM) | 13.8 billion years | expands faster and faster forever |
| Matter only, flat | 9.7 billion years | expands more and more slowly forever |
| Too much matter ($\Omega_m = 2{,}5$) | 7.8 billion years | expands to 1.67 times today’s size, then recollapses 54 billion years from now |
| Nearly empty ($\Omega_m = 0{,}05$) | 13.5 billion years | expands almost steadily |

> [Thử ngay] [[Real universe|thuc]] [[Matter only|vc]] [[Too much matter|dong]] [[Nearly empty|rong]]

A matter-only universe is **younger** than the oldest stars we measure (about 12–13 billion years): a contradiction. A nearly empty universe could not have formed the galaxies and clusters we see. ΛCDM is chosen because three independent kinds of data point to the same place: supernovae (accelerating expansion), the background radiation (flat space, $\Omega_m$ about 0.3) and the distribution of galaxies.

+++ Go deeper: a closed formula for the age
Neglecting radiation (which matters only for the first few tens of thousands of years), a flat universe with only matter and a cosmological constant has a closed-form solution:

$$ t_0 = \frac{2}{3H_0\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda}}\,\operatorname{arsinh}\sqrt{\frac{\Omega_\Lambda}{\Omega_m}} . $$

With $1/H_0 = 14{,}51$ billion years, $\Omega_\Lambda = 0{,}685$, $\Omega_m = 0{,}315$: $\sqrt{\Omega_\Lambda/\Omega_m} = 1{,}475$, $\operatorname{arsinh} 1{,}475 = 1{,}181$, so $t_0 = 14{,}51 \times \dfrac{2 \times 1{,}181}{3 \times 0{,}828} \approx 13{,}8$ billion years. The model in this lesson integrates numerically, including radiation, and gets 13.79 billion years.

When $\Omega_\Lambda = 0$, $\Omega_m = 1$: $t_0 = \dfrac{2}{3H_0} = 9{,}7$ billion years. A completely empty universe ($\Omega = 0$): $a$ grows steadily and $t_0 = 1/H_0 = 14{,}5$ billion years.
+++
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.ten: Getting it right, and open questions
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.noiDung:
The camera pulls back. The red-orange glass sphere is the {{mặt cầu Hubble|Hubble sphere}}: there the recession velocity $H_0 d$ equals $c$, at a radius $c/H_0 \approx 14{,}5$ billion light-years. Light from galaxies with $z$ greater than about 1.5 is reaching us from places that today are receding **faster than light**.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Receding faster than light violates relativity.” Special relativity forbids an object from overtaking a light ray **right next to it**. Recession velocity is the rate of growth of a very large distance, added up from the stretching of every stretch of space along the way. Nothing ever catches up with a light ray locally.

> [Hiểu sai thường gặp] “Everything expands: atoms, Earth, the Solar System.” No. Anything held together tightly by gravity or electromagnetic forces keeps its size; expansion shows up only between groups and clusters of galaxies that are no longer bound to each other. If the Earth–Sun distance grew at the rate $H_0$, it would increase by 10 m a year; Earth’s orbit does not grow like that. That is why the galaxies in the model keep their size.

> [Thử ngay] Drag the cosmic clock into the future: the Hubble sphere grows only to about 17.5 billion light-years and then nearly stops, while the distances to galaxies keep multiplying, so one by one they pass outside the sphere.
> [[Toggle the Hubble sphere|hubble]] [[At a = 0.5|qk]] [[Back to today|nay]]

**The Hubble tension.** Two ways of measuring $H_0$ disagree: from the background radiation through the ΛCDM model, Planck gives $67{,}4 \pm 0{,}5$; from the distance ladder (Cepheid variable stars, then supernovae), the SH0ES team measures $73 \pm 1$. That is an 8% gap, far larger than either side’s stated uncertainty. Another team using the James Webb Space Telescope with other kinds of stars in place of Cepheids finds about 70, in between. There may be undiscovered errors, or ΛCDM may be missing a piece of physics. The question is **still open**.

**Is dark energy really constant?** DESI data on the distribution of galaxies (2024–2025), combined with supernovae and the background radiation, **hint** that dark energy may be weakening over time. The evidence is not yet strong enough to be conclusive; the model in this lesson still uses a cosmological constant.

The next lesson draws this same universe as a spacetime diagram: our past light cone, the Hubble sphere, and the horizons that limit what we can ever see.
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.de: Drag the cosmic clock into the future (and move the sample galaxy if needed) until the sample galaxy sits right on the Hubble sphere: receding at exactly the speed of light (to within 0.04 c).
bai.baiGiang.buoc.8.thuThach.goiY: The original sample galaxy (now 3.3 billion light-years away) recedes at exactly $c$ when the universe is about 42 billion years old. Move it farther out and that moment comes sooner.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.2.y: $a$ is the scale factor when the light was emitted ($a = 1$ today).
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.3.y: $\rho$ includes matter, radiation and dark energy; $k$ is the curvature of space.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.4.y: About 5 hydrogen atoms per cubic meter. $\Omega = \rho/\rho_c$.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.5.y: Dark energy has $P = -\rho c^2$, so it makes the expansion accelerate.
bai.baiGiang.congThuc.6.y: Radiation dominated at first, then matter, and now dark energy.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.hoi: With $H_0 = 70$ km/s per megaparsec, how fast does a galaxy 200 Mpc away recede?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.1.giai: $v = H_0 d = 70 \times 200 = 14\,000$ km/s. The unit “km/s per megaparsec” means each megaparsec of distance adds 70 km/s of velocity.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.hoi: Someone in a galaxy 1 billion light-years from us looks out at the universe. What do they see?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.1: Every galaxy flying toward the Milky Way, the center of the expansion
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.2: Every other galaxy receding from them, faster the farther it is, just as we see
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.3: Half the sky receding, the other half approaching
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.chon.4: The galaxies standing still, because that observer is flying along with them
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.2.giai: The expansion $v = Hd$ has no center: from any galaxy you see the same law. The Milky Way is nothing special.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.hoi: Light was emitted when every large distance was only 1/4 of today’s. What is its redshift $z$?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.3.giai: $1 + z = 1/a = 4$, so $z = 3$. People often answer $z = 4$ by forgetting the 1, or $z = 0{,}25$ by taking $a$ directly.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.hoi: When $a = 0{,}5$, how many times larger than today were the matter density and the dark-energy density (cosmological constant)?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.4.giai: Matter thins out as $a^{-3}$: $0{,}5^{-3} = 8$. A cosmological constant does not thin out. A factor of 16 is what radiation does ($a^{-4}$).
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.hoi: Why does dark energy make the universe expand faster and faster, while matter slows the expansion down?
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.1: Because dark energy thins out faster than matter
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.2: Because its pressure is negative, $P = -\rho c^2$, so $\rho + 3P/c^2$ is negative and the acceleration equation gives $\ddot a > 0$
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.chon.3: Because it is a centrifugal force from the universe’s rotation
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.5.giai: The acceleration equation contains $\rho + 3P/c^2$. For matter $P \approx 0$ and the sum is positive: braking. For dark energy the sum is $-2\rho_\Lambda$: pushing. Dark energy does not thin out at all; it is not that it thins out faster.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.hoi: A friend says: “A galaxy at $z = 3$ is receding faster than light, so relativity is wrong. And if space expands, my desk should be getting bigger too.” Answer both points.
bai.baiGiang.cauHoi.6.dap: Special relativity only forbids overtaking a light ray at the same place. Recession velocity is the rate at which the distance to a very far place grows, because every stretch of space along the way is stretching; nothing overtakes a light ray beside it, so there is no contradiction. As for the desk: it, atoms, Earth, the Solar System and even galaxies are held tightly together by electromagnetic forces or gravity, so they keep their size; expansion shows up only between groups of galaxies that are no longer bound to each other.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.1: B. Ryden, *Introduction to Cosmology* (2nd ed., 2016): the Hubble law, a Newtonian derivation of the Friedmann equation, single- and multi-component universes, measuring cosmological parameters.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.2: J. B. Hartle, *Gravity: An Introduction to Einstein’s General Relativity* (2003), chapters 17–18: cosmology, the Friedmann–Robertson–Walker metric, the history of the expansion.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.3: Davis and Lineweaver 2004, “Expanding Confusion,” PASA 21, 97: faster-than-light recession, redshift, the Hubble sphere; clears up misconceptions one by one.
bai.baiGiang.docThem.4: Baez and Bunn 2005, “The Meaning of Einstein’s Equation,” Am. J. Phys. 73, 644: from $\rho + 3P/c^2$ to the acceleration equation of the universe.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.1.nghia: Recession velocity is proportional to distance: $v = H_0 d$. Derived by Lemaître in 1927; Hubble published the data in 1929.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.2.nghia: Einstein’s equation written for a homogeneous, isotropic universe: $H^2 = \tfrac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - kc^2/a^2$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.3.nghia: The density that makes space flat: $3H^2/(8\pi G)$, about $8{,}5 \times 10^{-27}$ kg/m³ today.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.4.nghia: The density of a component divided by the critical density. Today $\Omega_m \approx 0{,}315$, $\Omega_\Lambda \approx 0{,}685$.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.5.nghia: $\ddot a/a = -\tfrac{4\pi G}{3}(\rho + 3P/c^2)$: tells whether the expansion is speeding up or slowing down.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.6.nghia: Matter that emits no light and reveals itself only through gravity; about 27% of the energy of the universe, five times as much as ordinary matter.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.7.nghia: The explosion of a white dwarf; its true brightness is nearly always the same, so it serves as a “standard candle” for measuring distance.
bai.baiGiang.thuatNgu.8.nghia: The discrepancy between $H_0$ inferred from the background radiation (67.4) and $H_0$ measured with the distance ladder (about 73). Not yet resolved.
